stories.headline: Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centres disrupt key services, derail AI research
stories.title: Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centres disrupt key services, derail AI research
stories.summary: Moscow, Oct 22: Russia prides itself on its digital advances -- from an extensive e-commerce services sector to ambitious plans for developing artificial intelligence. But now, some of the key data centres at the heart of its technical prowess have been knocked out by Ukrainian drone attacks in the 4.5-year-old full-scale invasion, suffering damage that could take a long time to repair. Ukraine this month hit three main data centres belonging to tech giant Yandex, one for Russia's biggest bank, Sberbank, and one for social media platform VKontakte, the country's equivalent to Facebook. While Yandex, Sberbank and VKontakte are coy about the damage, people and businesses across Russia have reported widespread interruptions to cloud services. Banking, e-commerce, geolocation and ride-hailing services, as well as Alisa, Yandex's virtual assistant, and multimodal AI chatbots all have suffered lasting disruptions. The fallout even spread to Russia's judicial system, reportedly forcing arbitration courts to cancel or postpone sessions and cutting database access. Most experts predict repairing the damage could take months, if not years. Some warn that Moscow's aspirations to become a leader in AI development could be significantly set back. “This effectively sets Russia far behind in the AI race,” said Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society activist group. Data centres have been hit by both sides in the war Data centres are the latest targets of aerial campaigns waged by both sides against each other's vital infrastructure. Russian missiles and drones have pummelled Ukraine's power grid and other key sites, part of Kremlin efforts to weaken morale and resistance. Moscow stepped up those attacks as winter approaches, taking advantage of a shortage of US-supplied Patriot interceptors, whose stockpiles have been drained by Washington's war with Iran. Ukraine retaliated with waves of drone attacks against Russian oil refineries, triggering a massive fuel crisis and bringing the war home to millions of civilians. US President Donald Trump has blamed the attacks for higher global oil prices, which have escalated largely due to the US war in Iran. Earlier this month, Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import diesel oil, shocking Ukraine and its allies. Ukraine also hit huge warehouses for Russia's top online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon. Kyiv's attacks on Russian data centres closely followed Moscow's recent strikes on data centres in Ukraine, which disrupted the internet and TV broadcasts. On October 8, Ukrainian drones hit a Yandex data centre in Sasovo in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company's three supercomputers. A data centre in Kaluga was hit a day later and the one in Vladimir was struck October 11. The data centre and AI hub for Sberbank was hit October 14 in Balakovo in the Saratov region, and four days later, Kyiv struck a data centre in St. Petersburg serving VKontakte. Data centres are vulnerable While oil refineries and warehouses are easy prey, data centres are even softer targets -- massive buildings packed with servers and supporting power and cooling infrastructure. Lasting damage can result from a drone carrying a relatively light load of explosives. The vulnerability of data centres was exposed by Iran, whose drones hit two Amazon Web Services data centres in the United Arab Emirates and one in Bahrain. AWS said last month it was unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted at two of them. Yandex has run drills for an accident that could incapacitate one of its six data centres, but it was caught unprepared when its three key facilities were hit over four days. It wasn't immediately clear why air defences near the sites had failed. “The problem in Russia is that they've got to cover a big country with air defence and they don't have enough,” said Nick Reiners, senior geotechnology analyst at Eurasia Group. Russia's efforts to build a sovereign internet backfire Ukraine has stored critical data on servers in allied European countries, helping limit the damage from Russian attacks. But Moscow's strict digital sovereignty policy requires all data storage at home, making it extremely vulnerable. “Because all the infrastructure and all the data is located inside Russia, it's relatively easier to take down,” Reiners said. Klimarev predicted the data centre attacks could encourage many top Russian companies to move data abroad, while the authorities could ease their efforts to tighten internet controls to minimise the damage. “Paradoxically, the strikes on data centres have saved the Russian internet from isolation, as they will now have to move computing assets, most likely, to Europe,” Klimarev said. “It's quite likely that many Russian businesses are now roaming the European market to rent computing assets.” Russians are vexed by service disruptions Yandex dominates digital life in Russia and many former Soviet nations. It provides a wide variety of functions, including a search engine, cloud storage, payment apps, geolocation and ride-hailing services, and e-commerce platforms. “Yandex is kind of like Uber and Amazon and Google and everything rolled into one,” with everything "concentrated in just a few data centres,” Reiners said. “From a strategic perspective, they're an excellent target.” The attacks on Yandex caused unprecedented disruptions, paralysing payments, online orders, taxi rides and access to personal data. Moscow resident Igor Mann said he couldn't collect an order he placed with Yandex Market, an e-commerce platform. He said he tried using a virtual private network, but “nothing worked.” Taxi driver Pavel Belyavskiy, who gets orders via Yandex's ride-hailing app, couldn't connect with passengers. “On several orders already, I've ended up waiting for a long time and had to cancel the ride because I couldn't even get in touch with the passenger,” he said. The attacks also caused temporary disruptions at some major companies and banks that rely on Yandex cloud services. “It's not just about convenience -- it's also about work ... tied to everyday life,” said another Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko. A blow to Russia's AI ambitions Yandex said it restored most key cloud services in the following days as it turned to other data centres in Russia. But the damage to the company's AI development efforts is widely seen as massive and longer-lasting. Yandex has invested in huge data centres as the global AI boom fuels demand for computing power. The company's three supercomputers used to develop models are ranked among the top 500 in the world. Its most powerful computer -- at the Sasovo data centre -- was ranked 19th. Yandex didn't disclose the extent of the strikes' consequences, but satellite images indicated its data centres sustained serious damage. Some observers noted that fires triggered by the attacks probably seriously damaged high-end chips and other key equipment. “With this kind of hit, it's hard to expect that at least something was left intact -- the data centres' equipment is fragile, demanding and expensive,” Klimarev said. “Soot from the fire is bad for electronics.” While Russia already lagged years behind the US and China, “Ukraine's drone strikes will likely still set back Russian AI efforts further,” said Connor Martin, an expert with the Council for Foreign Relations. He said in a commentary that Russia likely will struggle to quickly replace the US-designed Nvidia A100 chips powering Yandex's supercomputers. Klimarev also said the global deficit of high-end chips, combined with the sanctions on their delivery to Russia, will make repairs long and costly. “I'm not sure it can be done in half a year, a year, or even at all,” he said.

stories.headline: India backs continuation of UN war crimes tribunal mechanism
stories.title: India backs continuation of UN war crimes tribunal mechanism
stories.summary: India has backed the continuation of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT), stressing that its residual functions remain vital for protecting victims and witnesses, preserving tribunal archives, and ensuring accountability for war crimes and genocide in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India has backed the continuation of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT), stressing that its residual functions remain vital for protecting victims and witnesses, preserving tribunal archives, and ensuring accountability for war crimes and genocide in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

United Nations: India backs keeping the mechanism established to continue the work of two international criminal tribunals, saying this would ensure continued accountability for the war crimes and genocide committed in the two regions.

“India underscores the importance of the mechanism continuing residual functions, including the protection of victims and witnesses, assistance to national jurisdictions, and the preservation and management of the tribunal’s archives”, Congress MP Manish Tiwari said on Wednesday (local time).
“These functions remain essential to safeguarding the legacy of the ad hoc tribunals and ensuring continued accountability”, he said.

He was speaking at a plenary session of the General Assembly on the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT), which was set up by the Security Council in 2010 to take on the unfinished work of the International Criminal Tribunals for Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

The Rwanda tribunal tried those responsible for the genocide of the Tutsis during a civil war and ended its work in 1994, while the Yugoslav tribunal that rendered justice on war crimes closed in 1993.
The Yugoslav tribunal held 111 trials and convicted 90 persons, one of whom has an appeal pending with the IRMCT.
The Rwanda tribunal indicted 86 persons in connection with the genocide of about 800,000 Tutsi ethnic group and some moderate Hutus by the Hutu extremists who controlled the government of Rwanda.
The IRMCT convicted 61 people after it picked up some of the cases from the tribunal.

“We recognise the mechanism’s contribution to the fight against impunity and reiterate the importance of fulfilling its mandate in accordance with the principles of justice, impartiality, fairness and due process, upholding the interests of justice and protecting the rights of victims remains essential”, Tiwari said.

As the IRMCT “moves towards completing its mandate, we emphasise the need for an efficient, orderly and time-bound transition without compromising judicial independence or the effective discharge of its remaining responsibilities”, he said.

stories.headline: Udhayanidhi says election petition against him was filed in Madras High Court after 45-day mark
stories.title: Udhayanidhi says election petition against him was filed in Madras High Court after 45-day mark
stories.summary: Justice G. Arul Murugan winds up hearing oral arguments on applications filed by the Leader of the Opposition to reject the election petition and strike off pleadings
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Tamil Nadu’s Leader of the Opposition (LoP) Udhayanidhi Stalin has contended before the Madras High Court that an election petition challenging his victory from the Chepauk-Thiruvallikeni Assembly constituency in the 2026 polls has been filed after the expiry of the statutory time limit of 45 days.

Appearing before Justice G. Arul Murugan, senior counsel P. Wilson urged the judge to reject the election petition at the threshold, without taking it up for trial, on the ground that it had been filed after the limitation period, prescribed under Section 81 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, ended.
The counsel said, the LoP had secured 62,992 votes as against his nearest rival candidate D. Selvam of the TVK, who got 55,852 votes.
The election petition had been filed by P. Milany of Theni district, who had also contested from the Chepauk-Thiruvallikeni constituency and secured 30 votes.
Highlighting that Mr. Udhayanidhi was declared elected on May 4, 2026, the counsel claimed the election petition challenging his victory ought to have been filed on or before June 17, 2026.
Since the present petition had been filed on June 18, 2026, he argued it was barred by limitation.
The counsel contended that the principle of excluding the first day, under the General Clauses Act of 1897, for the purpose of calculating limitation period would not apply to election petitions.
He underlined that Section 81 of the 1951 Act specifically uses the term “from the date of election of the returned candidate.”
“Normally, MiLord, Your Lordship knows that if a judgment is pronounced today, the limitation would begin only from the next day.
But the 1951 Act is a special legislation and it specifically states that an election petition must be presented within 45 days from the date of the election of the returned candidate,” he said.

The counsel said, the Election Commission of India (ECI) had also sent a communication to the Registrar General of the High Court confirming that the election petitions with respect to the 2026 general elections must be filed in the High Court on or before June 17, 2026.

He relied upon a Supreme Court judgment in Youaraj Rai versus Chander Bahadur (2006) and argued that the top court, too, had categorically held that the limitation period for filing an election petition would begin from the date of election of the returned candidate.

stories.headline: Indian-American Ramaswamy defends attack ad against rival Acton
stories.title: Indian-American Ramaswamy defends attack ad against rival Acton
stories.summary: Washington, Oct 22 : Indian-American Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign for Ohio governor is standing by a one-minute attack ad in which Democratic rival Amy Acton’s estranged birth mother calls her “a liar”, even as Vice President J.D. Vance rallied voters for him in suburban Cincinnati. The Ramaswamy campaign confirmed late on Tuesday that it had produced the ad featuring Donna Arthur, Acton’s birth mother, according to Axios and The Hill. Campaign spokesperson Connie Luck said Arthur was not paid and that the campaign would spend $4 million promoting the ad online and on television, the reports said. Acton has said she was removed from her mother at the age of 12 “for severe abuse and neglect, and sexual abuse,” according to reports by The Hill and WOUB. The ad drew sharp criticism. Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown called it “disgusting”, while commentator Meghan McCain described it as “dastardly”, the reports said. Casey Putsch, a former Republican rival of Ramaswamy, said he would vote for Acton. PolitiFact, which examined the ad’s claims on Wednesday, reviewed the dispute between Acton and her birth mother over her childhood. At a rally with Vance in Sharonville on Wednesday, Ramaswamy did not mention Acton at all, according to the Dayton Daily News. Instead, he pitched his plans for zero state income tax, lower electricity bills, property-tax cuts and support for the steel industry, the paper reported. Vance, however, defended the ad, saying the campaign “told it like it is”, according to public radio stations WYSO and WVXU. A heckler was removed from the event, the stations reported. On X, Ramaswamy accused Acton of “hiding from debate” and said she “bans cameras” at her events. He also posted a video titled “A strong message to Republicans” and shared a segment by broadcaster Megyn Kelly on Acton. The timing is significant. More than 676,000 Ohioans have already cast their ballots, according to the reports. A recent Marist poll has closely tracked the race. Former President Barack Obama is due to join Brown and Acton at a rally in Cleveland on October 24, WYSO reported, in a sign that Democrats see the governor’s race as competitive in a state that has trended Republican. Ramaswamy, a biotech entrepreneur born in Cincinnati to immigrant parents from Kerala, ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 2024 before endorsing Donald Trump. He briefly co-led the Department of Government Efficiency effort with Elon Musk before launching his bid for governor. Acton, a physician, served as director of the Ohio Department of Health during the early months of the Covid-19 pandemic. Ohio votes in the November 3 general election. --IANS

stories.headline: The Darkest Day in the History of Jammu & Kashmir
stories.title: The Darkest Day in the History of Jammu & Kashmir
stories.summary: CROSS ROADS No single event has shaped the uncertainty of the future that the people of Jammu & Kashmir (J&K) uncomfortably and hesitantly peek out towards than those that unfolded on 22 October 1947. In the din of the cacophony of voices parroting ad nauseam terms such as the Line of Control (LoC), the United Nations (UN) Resolutions on J&K, the Shimla Agreement, statehood for Gilgit Baltistan, Article 370 of India’s Constitution, and the like, the reason why these terms came into being in the first place has sadly long ceased to be a matter of interest to a vast majority of even those that deliberate publicly and vociferously on the plight of J&K. On that very day the seeds were sown for the physical tearing apart of J&K, for what we see today as the blurring of the identity of J&K and its people, for the destruction of the peaceful and inclusive way of life in the region and the crumbling of the long-held social values in J&K, and for the induction of the ugly head of terrorism into J&K by Pakistan. In essence, the roots of the hydra-headed predicament that J&K confronts today can indubitably be traced back to that one single event that commenced on that fateful autumn day. As gripping and intriguing as the history of the region in the period leading up to, and in the aftermath of, the events of October 1947 were, for the purpose of this piece, I shall restrict it to sketching the broad outlines. Maharaja Hari Singh, the Hindu Dogra ruler of Muslim-majority J&K at the time of India’s independence, seemed inclined towards independence and did not initially appear to be keen to join either dominion. On 12 August 1947, he therefore sought a standstill agreement with both India and Pakistan. stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 22 : Economists on Thursday maintained back-to-back repo rate hike stance, as the RBI MPC minutes for October revealed more hawkish tone, inclining towards future risk and policy tightening. A report by SBI Research said that it continues to maintain 50 bps rate hike in December, either through a “plain vanila” 50 bps repo rate hike or an “exotic” 50 bps rate hike with a 25-bps repo rate and a 25-bps asymmetric widening of the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) corridor (MSF at 6.25 per cent and SDF at 5.50 per cent). “The broadening of inflationary pressures, alongside persistent rupee weakness, calls for close monitoring by the RBI and a calibrated policy response to contain inflation risks and reinforce monetary transmission,” said Dr Soumya Kanti Ghosh, Group Chief Economic Adviser, State Bank of India. “We expect the peak inflation rate by November below 6.5 per cent and with these elevated levels, such generalisation warrants close monitoring by the RBI,” Dr Ghosh added. According to Radhika Rao, Senior Economist and Executive Director, DBS Bank, the minutes from the RBI’s October rate meeting reflected the hawkish pivot, where the repo rate was raised by 25 bp and stance was changed to ‘calibrated tightening’. “Members cited rising inflationary pressures and firm growth as reasons behind the 25bp hike. Tone of the commentary put two external members in the most hawkish camp, as they emphasised the broadening inflation risks and need for pre-emptive action, while two others were considered mildly hawkish/neutral as they supported only incremental hikes and explicitly rejected signalling a prolonged tightening cycle,” she explained. The RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra highlighted emerging signs of inflation becoming more generalised. With inflation set to rise to 6 per cent in CY Q4, “the door remains open for a back-to-back hike in December,” said Rao. In markets, bond yields stayed high, while the rupee was appreciated due to forex regulatory measures. As restrictions gained traction, the rupee has strengthened by around 1.5 per cent/USD this month, defying the usual headwinds from rising oil prices and subdued global risk sentiment, while FX forward premiums remain elevated. Inflows towards the country’s biggest-ever equity IPO also contributed to forex gains, said economists. For now, the currency is exhibiting limited reaction to external developments, while bonds are set to remain under pressure as oil supply fears return to the table, said Rao. --IANS

stories.headline: TPCI, UKIBC sign pact to boost India-UK trade ties
stories.title: TPCI, UKIBC sign pact to boost India-UK trade ties
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 22 : The Trade Promotion Council of India (TPCI) has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the UK-India Business Council (UKIBC) to deepen bilateral commercial ties following the entry into force of the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), it was announced on Thursday. The MoU between TPCI and UKIBC establishes a framework for institutional business collaboration. The partnership focuses on connecting businesses, facilitating trade missions, sharing market intelligence, and creating growth opportunities for Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) across both nations, according to a TPCI statement. In tandem with the MoU signing, TPCI also organised a B2B matchmaking showcase in London featuring 48 Indian exporting companies and 150 UK-based importers. The food and beverage sector represents a significant growth corridor under the new trade framework. Notably, the UK currently imports $50.68 billion worth of processed food annually with India's share at 0.6 per cent ($309.5 million), presenting significant room for expansion. Under CETA, UK tariffs of up to 70 per cent on processed foods, 4.2-8.5 per cent on shrimp, and duties on instant coffee have been eliminated. Mohit Singla, Chairman, TPCI, said, “This MoU is a major milestone in taking India-UK trade engagement from policy to partnership. Following the entry into force of the India-UK CETA, both TPCI and UKIBC will be deeply engaged in bilateral trade development, ensuring that the post-FTA momentum translates into tangible outcomes.” Singla further stated that with 99 per cent of Indian tariff lines now entering the UK duty-free, and peak tariffs of up to 70 per cent on processed foods eliminated under CETA, the landscape for Indian food exporters has transformed dramatically.” Apart from that, the TPCI team also held meetings with the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST), London Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) and the Scotch Whisky Association. “Both sides discussed business support while boosting international trade to drive economic growth,” according to TPCI. Moreover, bilateral trade between India and the UK reached 48 billion pounds ($65 billion) in FY2025-26. After this, Indian food exporters are poised to scale exports, expand beyond the 1.86 million Indian diaspora market and establish supply chains across UK retail and food service sectors. --IANS

stories.headline: Srinagar’s Sprawl is No Mark of Progress
stories.title: Srinagar’s Sprawl is No Mark of Progress
stories.summary: Srinagar is expanding, but it is not growing in the manner a city should. Its boundaries are spreading into villages, agricultural fields, wetlands and open spaces without a coherent urban vision to guide that transformation. What is being celebrated as development increasingly resembles uncontrolled sprawl—a disorderly outward march that is placing immense pressure on land, infrastructure and the environment. The city’s expansion is visible along every major approach road. New colonies, commercial structures and residential complexes are rising rapidly on the outskirts, often ahead of roads, drainage systems, public transport, schools and healthcare facilities. In several areas, construction has become the first sign of urban planning; civic services arrive later, if they arrive at all. This reverses the basic logic of responsible development. Srinagar’s geography makes such expansion particularly dangerous. The city is surrounded by wetlands, water channels, orchards and agricultural land that perform essential ecological functions. These spaces absorb excess water, moderate temperatures and sustain livelihoods. When they are filled, narrowed or built over, the consequences are not limited to the loss of scenery. Flooding becomes more severe, traffic congestion spreads, groundwater systems are disturbed and the city’s capacity to withstand extreme weather declines. The recurring expansion of built-up areas also exposes the weakness of enforcement. Master plans and zoning regulations have little meaning if violations are regularised after construction or if permissions are granted without assessing the cumulative impact on roads, drainage and public utilities. A city cannot be planned plot by plot while ignoring the combined pressure created by thousands of new structures. Urban sprawl also deepens inequality. Affluent developments may create private access roads and independent services, while ordinary residents in peripheral colonies are left with inadequate transport, poor waste collection, unreliable drainage and limited public amenities. The result is a city that becomes larger but not more liveable. Srinagar urgently needs a transparent and enforceable urban growth strategy. Construction on wetlands, flood channels and prime agricultural land must face strict scrutiny. Public transport and compact, mixed-use development should be prioritised over endless low-density expansion. Local bodies must be equipped with updated maps, technical staff and the authority to act against illegal construction—regardless of influence. The question is not whether Srinagar should develop. It must. The question is whether development will serve the city or slowly destroy the conditions that make it habitable. If urban growth continues without ecological restraint and civic planning, Srinagar will inherit the worst features of a metropolis without gaining the benefits of one. Progress cannot mean covering every available piece of land with concrete. A liveable Srinagar must be planned before it is permitted to spread beyond repair.
